subject: Banking
title: Selling Your Data
description: A quick, practical guide to Selling Your Data.

hook.text: Your bank knows every purchase you make. That spending data is valuable to advertisers, retailers, and data brokers.

buildup.text: Banks anonymize and aggregate transaction data. They sell spending trends to hedge funds, retailers.

discovery.text: A hedge fund can predict a company's quarterly revenue by analyzing credit card spending data.

twist.text: Banks claim data is anonymized. But with enough data points, individuals can often be re-identified from spending.

climax.text: Your transaction history is a product. You are the source, advertisers are the buyers, and the bank is the broker.

punchline.text: Banks sell your spending data. You're the product, not just the customer.

quiz.question: Who buys anonymized bank transaction data?
options: Hedge funds, retailers, and marketing firms

details.summary: Banks monetize customer transaction data by selling aggregated and anonymized insights to marketers, retailers, and data brokers. Your spending patterns reveal lifestyle habits that are valuable to advertisers and marketing companies.
details.whyItMatters: Most bank customers do not realize their transaction data has commercial value beyond banking. Understanding data monetization reveals an often-invisible revenue stream that banks build from your financial activity.
takeaways: Banks sell anonymized transaction data to retailers and marketers
Spending data reveals income levels, shopping habits, and lifestyle choices
Some banks offer opt-out options but few customers know about them

faq.question: What type of data do banks sell?
faq.answer: Banks typically sell aggregated and anonymized data showing spending trends by demographic, location, and merchant category. Individual transaction records are generally not sold directly, but the patterns they reveal about groups of consumers are highly valuable.

faq.question: Can you stop your bank from selling your data?
faq.answer: Federal law requires banks to provide opt-out options for some data sharing. However, many types of aggregated data sharing do not require consent. Reading your bank's privacy notice and opting out of marketing data sharing provides partial protection.
